dohori.window: Village sung duels from at least the 19th century (no source gives a year); on Radio Nepal and record from the late 1970s and 1980s; a commercial cassette, VCD and YouTube industry from the late 1990s, after Nepal Television's 'Lok Dohori' programme (1998) and the dohori sanjh restaurants
dohori.sound: Nepal's sung duel: two sides, usually young men against young women, trade improvised rhyming couplets as question and answer over the repeated tune and refrain of a well-known folk song, to the beat of the madal drum, often with harmonium and sarangi; rooted in the Gurung rodhi ghar courting evenings of the central hills, and on record a lively, tightly arranged male-female duet whose lyrics move from love and teasing to migration, politics and Tij-festival protest.
markers: A male and a female voice answering each other couplet by couplet, each reply rhymed to the last
One repeated folk tune and refrain carrying many verses, the lyric changing with each question and answer
The madal hand drum driving a dancing beat, with harmonium or sarangi filling between couplets
Teasing, witty Nepali verse full of place names, proverbs, plants and animals used for the rhyme
near: Tamang selo: the Tamang community's song, usually carried by the damphu frame drum with madal and tungna, sung to its own selo tunes; not the hill-Nepali two-team duel of improvised couplets that dohori is
Nepali adhunik geet (sugam sangeet): a composed, slow, poetic solo song with harmonium and strings, not an improvised question-and-answer duet

tamangselo.window: c. 1800 onward (tree date; no page read dates the start). First recordings: Hira Devi Waiba's Radio Nepal songs of 1966 and HMV albums of 1974 and 1978; cassette albums from the 1990s; a large flow of digital singles 2023 onward.
tamangselo.sound: The song and dance of the Tamang people of the hills around the Kathmandu Valley (Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Sindhupalchok, Kavre) and of the Nepali-speaking hills of Darjeeling and Sikkim: a brisk, rhythmic folk song driven by the damphu frame drum with madal and the tungna lute, sung for Lhosar, weddings and gatherings about love, sorrow, humour and everyday life, often as a call between singers, and since the 1990s also set to drum kit, guitar and keyboards in Nepali pop.
markers: The damphu, a large tambourine-like frame drum with 32 pegs, setting a bouncing dance pulse
Madal hand drum and the plucked tungna lute beside the damphu
Short, catchy sung verses about love, sorrow and village life, lively or slow, often traded between a man and a woman
Tamang words and names in the lyrics (maichyang, chyangba, syangbo) and Lhosar themes
near: Sung question-and-answer folk duet from the dohori saanjh circuit, a performer known for dohori, not a damphu-led Tamang selo
Kathmandu modern song (adhunik geet) with harmonium, sitar and flute, a lyrical solo ballad, not Tamang village song on the damphu

pasillo.window: c. 1830 onward (tree date; pages read put its birth in the first decades of the 19th century, in the Andes of New Granada during the independence wars; in Ecuador from the 1870s; the sung pasillo from the 1910s; still recorded in 2026)
pasillo.sound: A fast or slow song and dance in 3/4 adapted from the European waltz in Colombia and Ecuador. In Colombia it is either an instrumental pasillo fiestero for bandola, tiple and guitar (or piano) with spoon percussion, or a slow sung pasillo for two voices with string accompaniment. In Ecuador it became the national song: slow, melancholic, in low keys, setting modernist poems about lost love, sung by duets and later trios with requinto guitar.
markers: Three-beat (3/4) waltz time, quick and dance-like in Colombia, slow and dragging in Ecuador
Two voices in parallel thirds over guitars, or an instrumental lead on bandola, tiple or piano
Ecuadorian pasillos: a slow, mournful minor-key melody setting a poem of loss and longing
Colombian pasillo fiestero: quick instrumental dance pieces with spoon (cucharas) percussion
near: A Colombian bambuco by Jorge Villamil, sung by the same duo as pasillos, but in the bambuco's 6/8 feel and named a bambuco
A three-beat waltz-song too, but a Peruvian vals criollo by Chabuca Granda from Lima's criollo tradition, not the Andean pasillo

meringue.window: c. 1850 onward (tree date; English Wikipedia gives mid-19th century; earliest recordings found are the Lomax field recordings of 1936-37; largely absorbed into kompa from the mid-1950s)
meringue.sound: Haiti's national song and dance: a lilting, unhurried couple dance in duple time built on the five-note quintolet (the Cuban cinquillo, 'dak-ta-dak-ta-dak'), played on strings, piano and horns rather than the Dominican accordion and sung in Haitian Creole or French. It ranges from the slow, caressing salon or concert méringue for solo piano (Lamothe, the Duroseaus), through the quicker dance méringue of the 1940s-50s Port-au-Prince orchestras, to the excited, satirical carnival méringue.
markers: The five-note quintolet / cinquillo figure (long-short-long-short-long) running under the melody
Strings, piano and horns, not accordion: guitar and saxophone orchestras or a solo salon piano
A slower, swaying, nostalgic tempo than Dominican merengue, with Creole or French vocals
near: Dominican merengue: the big-band orquesta version of the accordion-and-tambora dance from the other side of Hispaniola, faster and in a straight driving 2/4, not the string-and-piano Haitian méringue
Konpa (compas direct), the 1955 modernisation of méringue by Nemours Jean-Baptiste: a steady mid-tempo groove with a constant cowbell or cymbal pulse and electric guitars, filed as its own genre

gaitazuliana.window: 1850 onward (tree date; es.wikipedia places the origins perhaps in the first decades of the 19th century; first recordings in the late 1940s, national popularity from the 1960s)
gaitazuliana.sound: The Christmas-season song of Zulia state, Venezuela: a solo singer trades four-line coplas with a mixed chorus singing the estribillo over a 6/8 swing, carried by the cuatro, the friction drum furro (furruco) as bass, maracas, the metal scraper charrasca and the tambora; sung to the Virgin of Chiquinquirá, to Maracaibo and in protest, from the 1960s conjuntos to the tamborera and salsa-touched bands of the 1970s.
markers: A furro friction drum giving a groaning bass pulse
Strummed cuatro and the rasping metal charrasca on a 6/8 swing
A solo copla answered by a full mixed-voice chorus
Lyrics to the Virgin of Chiquinquirá, Maracaibo and political protest
fits: La máxima expresión de la gaita zuliana (album)
near: Colombian gaita: the Caribbean-coast cumbia of the gaita flute, a different instrument and tradition that only shares the name
Venezuelan plains joropo, harp-and-cuatro music of the llanos, not the furro-and-chorus Christmas song of Maracaibo

pasodoble.window: c. 1850 onward (tree date; Spanish Wikipedia dates pasodoble scores to 1780 as an infantry march and puts it in the bullring only in the 19th century; the oldest piece here, La Gracia de Dios, is from 1880; the first recordings found are España cañí by the Banda del Regimiento de Ingenieros de Madrid, 1926)
pasodoble.sound: Spain's quick march in binary time, played by bandas de música in the bullring, in Moros y Cristianos and Fallas parades and at village dances: an introduction on the dominant, a first strain in the home key and a 'trío' that comes back loud to close, often with an Andalusian, flamenco-tinged turn. Taurino pasodobles are the slowest, popular ones the fastest, and from the 1910s copla singers sang it as the pasodoble canción about toreros, Andalusia and Spain.
markers: A brisk two-beat march pulse (binary time, one step per beat) from a full wind band with snare and bass drum
Introduction, a first strain in the home key, then a 'trío' that is replayed loud as the climax
An Andalusian, flamenco-tinged melody, often in a minor key (Suspiros de España)
In the sung pasodoble canción, a copla singer telling of toreros, bullfights and Andalusian or Spanish pride over the same march beat
fits: Unidad de Música de la Guardia Real
near: A sevillana in three-beat time (3/4) sung by a guitar-and-voice rociero group for pair dancing at fairs, not a two-beat band march
La verbena de la Paloma: ¿Dónde vas con mantón de Manila?

A sung scene from an 1894 género chico zarzuela, operatic voices and orchestra in a stage work; pasodobles grew partly out of this theatre, but this is a theatre number, not a march for band or bullring

harana.window: From the 1800s (Spanish era; the tree's 1850 is a judgement, no source gives a year); at its height before the Second World War and on 1940s-50s radio and records; the custom has declined since the 1980s and lives on in revival recordings (The Art of Harana 2003, the Harana Kings 2012).
harana.sound: The Filipino courtship serenade: a young man, often with friends, sings love songs under a woman's window at night to his own or a companion's guitar. The songs are mostly danzas in a 2/4 habanera rhythm and a major key, opened by a solo guitar introduction with a guitar interlude between verses, in pure and archaic Tagalog (or Ilocano, Cebuano and other languages) that places the singer in the act of serenading. Haranistas also sang kundiman, which is a related but distinct 3/4 art song.
markers: A lilting 2/4 habanera (danza) rhythm on one or two guitars
A solo guitar introduction and a guitar interlude between the verses
A lone tender male voice, crooning, addressing a beloved at her window at night
Lyrics in old-fashioned, formal Tagalog or another Philippine language, pleading for love
fits: The Art of Harana: Serenades for Guitar (album)
near: A 1990s rock-band song about serenading: its title names harana, but it has none of the habanera rhythm or the solo guitar-and-voice form
A patriotic kundiman in slow triple time sung by the same crooner, not a courtship serenade

jiangnansizhu.window: 1860 onward (Chinese Wikipedia: in vogue from 1860; Shanghai the centre by the early 20th century; the name fixed in the 1950s); still played by amateur clubs and conservatories
jiangnansizhu.sound: The amateur instrumental ensemble music of the lower Yangzi (southern Jiangsu, Shanghai, northern Zhejiang), played in teahouses and music clubs: a small, unfixed group of silk strings and bamboo winds (erhu, the long qudi flute or xiao, pipa and yangqin at the core, with sanxian, qinqin, sheng and a clapper) works a small body of old melodies, above all the Eight Great Pieces, each player ornamenting the same tune in a gentle heterophony where one fills in as another thins out.
markers: A soft, legato qudi or xiao flute and an erhu sharing the lead in the same melody
Heterophony: pipa, yangqin and sanxian each decorate one tune at once ("you busy, me simple")
One old melody heard in plain, slow and ornamented forms (Lao liu ban, Man liu ban, Zhong hua liu ban)
Chamber scale: two to ten players, one of each instrument, only a clapper and small drum for percussion
fits: Lu Chunling, Zhou Hui, Zhou Hao & Ma Shenglong
Jiangnan Sizhu: Beautiful Traditional Music from Southeastern China (album)
near: Nie Er's 1934 arrangement of the fast end of the sizhu piece Yang Ba Qu, played by a large conducted national orchestra from a full score, not a small club ensemble improvising ornament
Lü Wencheng's Cantonese piece led by the high gaohu fiddle, from the Guangdong silk-and-bamboo tradition, not the Jiangnan one
